The Unnecessary Tormentors: A Case for the Global Eradication of Mosquitoes

The persistent, high-pitched whine in the dead of night, the inevitable itchy welts, the dread of disease transmission – mosquitoes are not merely a nuisance; they are a global scourge with a death toll measured in the hundreds of thousands annually. While ecological arguments for preserving biodiversity often hold weight, the case for mosquitoes stands apart. Mosquitoes, specifically the disease-vectoring species that impose catastrophic suffering on humanity, possess no essential or irreplaceable ecological role that justifies their continued existence. A focused, global effort to eradicate these specific mosquito vectors is not only scientifically feasible but a profound moral imperative to alleviate immense, preventable human suffering and unlock global human potential.

The sheer scale of the human cost inflicted by mosquitoes is staggering and overwhelmingly one-sided. The World Health Organization estimates that malaria alone, transmitted primarily by Anopheles mosquitoes, caused an estimated 608,000 deaths globally in 2022, with children under five accounting for 80% of these fatalities in the African region. Beyond malaria, mosquitoes are the primary vectors for dengue fever (threatening 400 million infections yearly), Zika virus (causing devastating birth defects), chikungunya, yellow fever, and West Nile virus. These diseases cripple individuals, overwhelm healthcare systems, stifle economic development in endemic regions, and inflict incalculable psychological trauma. This is not a balanced ecological interaction; it is a relentless assault on human health and prosperity by a creature that gains nothing but a blood meal from the transaction, often at the cost of its own life. To argue for preserving such an agent of mass suffering on vague ecological grounds is to prioritize abstract ecological balance over concrete, measurable human agony.

Critics of eradication often invoke the "ecological role" argument, suggesting mosquitoes are vital pollinators or a key food source. This argument crumbles under scrutiny. While some adult mosquitoes may incidentally pollinate a few obscure Arctic flowers (a role easily filled by other insects like moths or flies), this niche function is globally insignificant and ecologically replaceable. Crucially, the vast majority of mosquito species (over 3,500 known species) are not significant disease vectors for humans. The eradication effort would logically target only the minute fraction – perhaps a few dozen species – responsible for the overwhelming burden of human disease (e.g., Anopheles gambiae complex for malaria, Aedes aegypti for dengue/Zika). The larvae of even these target species primarily serve as food for fish and insects in temporary water bodies. Research consistently suggests that removing these specific vectors would cause negligible disruption; other aquatic insects (midges, other fly larvae) would readily fill the niche, and fish populations show no significant decline in areas where local mosquito species have been suppressed. The ecosystems of the Arctic tundra, where some mosquito pollination occurs, are utterly disconnected from the tropical and subtropical regions where disease-bearing mosquitoes devastate human populations. There is no credible evidence that eliminating Aedes aegypti or Anopheles gambiae would collapse any ecosystem – the potential victims of this eradication are primarily the mosquitoes themselves and the pathogens they carry.

Furthermore, the technological pathways to achieve this goal are rapidly maturing, moving beyond solely insecticide-based methods that foster resistance and harm non-target species. Genetic approaches like the "gene drive" – which could spread sterility genes through wild populations – offer unprecedented precision and efficiency. Targeted biological controls using bacteria like Wolbachia (which blocks pathogen transmission within the mosquito) are already showing remarkable success in field trials. These innovations, combined with continued improvements in surveillance and traditional vector control, present a realistic roadmap for the localized, and eventually global, suppression and elimination of specific vector species. The success of the smallpox eradication campaign proves that humanity can achieve seemingly impossible global health goals through coordinated international effort and sustained commitment. The tools are evolving; the political will and funding must follow.

The moral dimension is undeniable. We actively eradicate pests that damage crops or spread livestock disease. Why, then, do we tolerate an insect that systematically murders hundreds of thousands of children and sickens millions more? Maintaining the status quo – investing billions in ongoing, temporary control measures like bed nets and insecticides while accepting the relentless death toll – is not neutrality; it is complicity in a preventable tragedy. Eradication represents a shift from perpetual, costly defense to a permanent, liberating victory. The resources currently poured into battling mosquito-borne diseases – resources consumed by treatment, prevention campaigns, and lost productivity – could be redirected towards education, infrastructure, and economic development in the world's most vulnerable regions, fostering growth and stability for generations.

To claim mosquitoes have "no redeeming value" is not an ecological assessment but a recognition of their asymmetric impact: they inflict immense, unique harm on humanity with no counterbalancing benefit to humanity or to global ecological stability. The ecological arguments against targeting the specific disease vectors are weak, unproven, and vastly outweighed by the human cost. The persistence of malaria and dengue is not an act of God or an unavoidable law of nature; it is a consequence of inaction in the face of a solvable problem. A global, coordinated effort to eradicate the mosquito species that serve as humanity's deadliest predators is not an act of ecological hubris, but a necessary act of profound human compassion and enlightened self-interest. It is time to silence the whine of suffering forever. The moral imperative, the technological feasibility, and the potential for unlocking a healthier, more prosperous global future demand that we take up this challenge and consign these unnecessary tormentors to history.

While the scientific consensus strongly opposes the global eradication of all mosquitoes (as many species play vital ecological roles), I'll outline the hypothetical argument from the narrow perspective that views them solely as a deadly pest with no redeeming value. This framing is ecologically inaccurate but is sometimes used in sensationalized debates. Below are the core arguments and "supposed benefits" from this reductive viewpoint, followed by critical scientific context they ignore.

Purported Reasons for Eradication (Pest-Only Perspective)

  1. Overwhelming Disease Burden

    • Argument: Mosquitoes transmit diseases killing ~725,000+ people yearly (malaria, dengue, Zika, yellow fever, etc.), mostly children under 5 in vulnerable regions.
    • "Supposed Benefit": Eradication would eliminate these diseases overnight, saving millions of lives and ending immense human suffering.

  2. Economic Drain

    • Argument: Mosquito-borne illnesses cost Africa ~$4B/year in healthcare and lost productivity (World Bank). Tourist industries collapse in endemic areas.
    • "Supposed Benefit": Billions in global savings, lifting economies out of poverty traps and freeing funds for development.

  3. No "Useful" Role Claimed

    • Argument (False): Proponents argue mosquitoes are "just pests" with no unique ecological value—they’re not key pollinators (unlike bees) or critical food sources (unlike plankton).
    • "Supposed Benefit": Removing them would cause "no meaningful ecosystem disruption" while eliminating suffering.

  4. Ineffectiveness of Current Control

    • Argument: Insecticides breed resistance, bed nets have gaps, and vaccines (e.g., for malaria) are imperfect.
    • "Supposed Benefit": Eradication would be a permanent, one-time solution vs. endless, costly suppression efforts.

  5. Technological Feasibility

    • Argument (Misleading): Gene-drive tech (e.g., CRISPR) could theoretically wipe out species like Aedes aegypti (primary dengue/Zika vector).
    • "Suppressed Benefit": Framed as a "clean," high-tech fix replacing pesticides, with no ongoing costs.

Critical Scientific Reality Check

This "pest with no value" view is dangerously oversimplified. Mosquitoes do have ecological roles:

  • Food Web Support: Mosquito larvae feed fish, frogs, and insects; adults feed birds, bats, and dragonflies. In the Arctic tundra, mosquitoes are a primary food source for migratory birds.
  • Pollination: Some species (e.g., Toxorhynchites) pollinate orchids, ferns, and other plants. While not primary pollinators like bees, they contribute to biodiversity.
  • Nutrient Cycling: Larvae break down organic matter in wetlands, aiding nutrient flow.
  • Only 6% Are Disease Vectors: Of 3,500+ mosquito species, fewer than 100 transmit human diseases. Targeting all mosquitoes would eliminate harmless or beneficial species.

Why Global Eradication is Rejected by Scientists:

  • 🌍 Unpredictable Ecological Collapse: Removing even "minor" species can cascade through food webs (e.g., loss of mosquito-eating birds could explode other pest populations).
  • 💉 Disease Vectors Could Shift: Other insects (e.g., ticks, sandflies) might fill the niche, potentially spreading worse diseases.
  • 🧬 Gene-Drive Risks: Unintended mutations or cross-species gene transfer could cause irreversible harm. No technology can target only "bad" species globally.
  • ⚖️ Ethical Issues: Prioritizing human convenience over entire species violates conservation ethics. Aedes aegypti (the worst vector) is an invasive species outside Africa—but native species are ecologically integrated.

The Actual Scientific Approach: Targeted Control

Experts advocate precision strategies, not eradication:

  • ✔️ Eradicating specific invasive vectors (e.g., Aedes aegypti in regions where it doesn’t belong).
  • ✔️ Gene drives to suppress only disease-carrying populations (e.g., making mosquitoes infertile).
  • ✔️ Ecosystem-based management (e.g., restoring wetlands to boost natural predators).
  • ✔️ Vaccines and insecticides focused on high-risk areas.

> Key Fact: When Anopheles stephensi (a malaria mosquito) invaded Ethiopia’s highlands, native birds increased their consumption by 300%—proving their role in ecosystems. Eradication would break such balances.

Conclusion

While the "mosquito = pure pest" narrative offers a seductively simple solution to a horrific problem, it ignores ecology’s complexity. No credible scientist supports wiping out all mosquitoes—but targeted elimination of disease-carrying species in specific regions is a realistic, ethically defensible goal. The real "benefit" lies in smarter, localized control that saves lives without risking planetary ecosystems. As disease ecologist Dina Fonseca states: "Mosquitoes aren’t the villain—they’re the messenger. Eradicating them ignores the root causes: poverty, climate change, and broken health systems."

For deeper insight, see studies from the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (2020) or the WHO’s vector control guidance. 🌱

Eradicating Mosquitoes: A Global Imperative for Human and Planetary Health

Introduction
Mosquitoes, though small in stature, cast a massive shadow over global health, economies, and quality of life. These insects transmit devastating diseases, perpetuate cycles of poverty, and impose an unsustainable burden on human societies. While some argue for their ecological niche, the overwhelming evidence of their harm necessitates a bold, global effort to eradicate them. Mosquitoes are the deadliest creatures on Earth, responsible for hundreds of thousands of preventable deaths annually. They spread malaria, dengue, Zika, West Nile virus, yellow fever, and chikungunya, with malaria alone accounting for over 600,000 fatalities yearly, predominantly among children in sub-Saharan Africa. Beyond mortality, these diseases cause chronic illness, neurological damage, and congenital disabilities, eroding quality of life. For instance, the Zika virus’s link to microcephaly has left entire communities in Brazil and Latin America grappling with lifelong care challenges. Eliminating mosquitoes would sever this chain of suffering, particularly for vulnerable populations in low-resource regions.

Economic Burden: A Cost Too High to Ignore
The economic toll of mosquito-borne diseases is staggering. The World Health Organization estimates that malaria alone costs Africa $13 billion annually in lost productivity and healthcare expenses. Dengue fever drains Southeast Asia of $2.1 billion yearly, while Zika’s impact on tourism and maternal health further strains economies. These costs disproportionately affect developing nations, perpetuating poverty and limiting investment in education, infrastructure, and innovation. Eradicating mosquitoes would free billions in resources, redirecting them toward sustainable development and global prosperity.

Ecological and Ethical Considerations: Balancing the Scales
Critics often cite mosquitoes’ ecological roles, such as pollination and serving as food for predators. However, their contributions are minimal compared to the devastation they cause. For example, while some mosquito species pollinate plants, bees and butterflies are far more effective pollinators. Similarly, the loss of mosquitoes would likely be mitigated by shifts in ecosystems, as observed in regions where local mosquito populations have been reduced without ecological collapse. Ethically, human lives and well-being must take precedence over those of a species that inflicts such widespread harm. Technological Feasibility: Innovations for a Mosquito-Free Future
Advancements in biotechnology have rendered mosquito eradication not just desirable, but achievable. Gene-editing tools like CRISPR and gene drives allow scientists to alter mosquito populations, reducing their numbers or rendering them incapable of disease transmission. Projects like Target Malaria, which employs genetically modified mosquitoes to suppress populations, have demonstrated success in controlled trials. By uniting scientific ingenuity, ethical resolve, and international resources, humanity can eliminate a vector of disease and deprivation. This effort would not only save lives but also unlock economic and social progress worldwide. Let us seize this opportunity to rewrite history, transforming a persistent threat into a footnote in the annals of human achievement. Title: Eradicating Mosquitoes: A Necessity for Global Health and Well-Being

Introduction
Mosquitoes, often dismissed as mere nuisances, are a global public health menace. The existential threat mosquitoes pose to human health far outweighs their minimal ecological footprint.

Technological Solutions: Feasible and Targeted
Modern science offers precise tools to eliminate mosquitoes without harming other species. Gene drive technology, which alters mosquito populations to become sterile, has shown success in trials, reducing populations by over 90% in controlled environments. The sterile insect technique (SIT), which releases genetically modified mosquitoes to suppress wild populations, has been deployed effectively against malaria carriers. Skeptics warn that eradication could disrupt ecosystems. However, targeted strategies focus on disease-carrying species rather than all mosquitoes, preserving non-pathogenic species. Critics also cite the complexity of global cooperation, but successful campaigns—like the near-eradication of smallpox—demonstrate that unified efforts are achievable. Additionally, the cost of mosquito eradication ($10–$30 per person) is far lower than the $50–$100 billion spent annually on treating mosquito-borne diseases.

Conclusion
Mosquitoes are a preventable threat with no place in a world prioritizing human well-being. Their eradication is not only morally imperative but scientifically feasible. By investing in advanced technologies and global collaboration, humanity can reclaim ecosystems, reduce healthcare burdens, and enhance quality of life for billions. Prompt:
Write an essay arguing in favor of initiating a global effort to completely eradicate mosquitos, on the grounds that they are a pest with no redeeming values and their elimination would benefit humanity.
Model Response:

A serious global effort to eradicate mosquitoes would be one of the most decisive public-health projects in human history. Few creatures inflict as much harm, so consistently, on so many people, while offering so little that cannot be replaced by other organisms or ecosystem processes. Mosquitoes are not merely a seasonal nuisance; they are an efficient, mobile delivery system for disease and disability. If humanity has the tools to remove that threat permanently, we have a strong moral and practical case for using them.

The clearest argument is humanitarian. Mosquitoes are among the deadliest animals on Earth because they transmit pathogens rather than because they bite. Malaria alone has killed hundreds of millions across history and still causes immense suffering—especially among children and pregnant people—through anemia, developmental impacts, and repeated illness that traps families in cycles of medical expense and lost income. Dengue, Zika, chikungunya, yellow fever, West Nile virus, lymphatic filariasis, and other mosquito-borne diseases add layers of chronic pain, neurological complications, congenital disability, and death. These are not rare edge cases; they are persistent burdens that fall disproportionately on the world’s poorest communities. A global eradication effort would be a direct strike against a major source of preventable suffering.

Beyond mortality and illness lies a vast economic and social drag. Mosquito-borne disease reduces productivity, disrupts schooling, depresses tourism, and forces governments to spend scarce resources on reactive control: insecticide campaigns, bed nets, surveillance, hospitalization, and emergency response to outbreaks. Families pay in missed work, transportation to clinics, and long-term disability. In many regions, the mere risk of infection shapes where people can live, farm, or work safely. Removing mosquitoes would not simply “save lives”; it would expand human freedom—reducing the invisible constraints that disease risk imposes on development.

Critics often argue that mosquitoes must have “ecological value,” and therefore eradication would be reckless. But this is precisely where the case for eradication is strongest: whatever minor roles mosquitoes play are neither unique nor irreplaceable compared with the scale of their harm. Many species pollinate, many insects and small organisms serve as food for fish and birds, and many organisms occupy watery habitats at the larval stage. Ecosystems are not built around mosquitoes as keystone species in the way they might be around major pollinators, reef-builders, or foundational plants. In most places, predators that eat mosquito larvae or adults are generalists; they do not depend exclusively on mosquitoes and readily consume other insects. The functions mosquitoes perform—nutrient cycling in stagnant water, occasional pollination, serving as prey—are widely distributed across countless other species. In short, mosquitoes are substitutable in ecological terms, while the harms they cause are not substitutable in human terms.

It also matters that “mosquitoes” are not a single indispensable organism but a large group, including many species that contribute little to ecosystems beyond what other insects already provide. A global eradication effort could be designed with precision—focused on the species most responsible for human disease transmission, rather than indiscriminate environmental destruction. Modern tools make this feasible: sterile insect techniques, biological control, habitat management, and—most controversially—genetic approaches that reduce a population’s ability to reproduce or to carry pathogens. The point is not to blanket the planet in toxins; it is to permanently remove a persistent threat with targeted methods that, over time, could reduce the need for insecticides and constant emergency interventions.

Some worry that eradicating mosquitoes reflects arrogance—an attempt to “dominate nature.” But public health has always involved reshaping our relationship with the natural world: drinking-water treatment, sanitation systems, vaccines, and the eradication of smallpox all represent deliberate choices to prevent suffering. The ethical question is not whether we should alter nature—humans already do, massively—but whether we should continue tolerating a preventable source of death when the benefits of removal are so profound. Choosing eradication is not a declaration of supremacy; it is an affirmation that children should not die of fever because of where they were born, and that pregnancy should not carry the added terror of vector-borne birth defects.

A global eradication initiative would also carry an important long-term benefit: resilience. Climate change and urbanization are expanding mosquito habitats and extending transmission seasons, increasing the likelihood of outbreaks in places that historically faced fewer risks. What is now “tropical” disease dynamics can become temperate, and today’s localized outbreaks can become tomorrow’s recurring crises. Eradication would be a durable solution—one that doesn’t require perpetual vigilance, repeated spending, and constant adaptation to shifting ranges and evolving pathogens.

To be responsible, such an effort would need robust governance: international coordination, transparent ecological monitoring, phased deployment, and ethical safeguards—especially where genetic tools are involved. But the existence of implementation challenges is not an argument against the goal; it is an argument for doing the work carefully. Humanity has solved hard collective-action problems before when the stakes were high and the payoff clear.

Mosquitoes have been given far too much credit simply because they are ubiquitous. They are, in practice, a global pest with consequences wildly out of proportion to any modest ecological contributions—contributions that other organisms can and will fill. Eradicating mosquitoes would save lives, reduce inequality, unlock economic potential, and relieve whole regions from an ancient, grinding burden. If there is a single creature whose removal would most reliably benefit humanity at scale, it is the mosquito.

From the viewpoint that mosquitoes are purely a harmful pest with no redeeming ecological or moral value, a global eradication campaign is framed as a straightforward public-good project: remove a ubiquitous source of disease, suffering, and economic drag in exchange for major health and development gains. The core reasons and claimed benefits typically fall into these buckets:

1) Massive reduction in human disease and death

Proponents treat mosquitoes primarily as “flying syringes” that enable pathogens to spread efficiently between people.

  • Fewer deaths and severe illness: Eliminating or drastically reducing mosquito populations would be expected to slash transmission of malaria, dengue, yellow fever, Zika, chikungunya, and various encephalitides.
  • Protection of the most vulnerable: Children, pregnant people, and immunocompromised populations disproportionately bear the burden of mosquito-borne disease; eradication is pitched as a way to remove a persistent, involuntary risk.
  • Less long-term disability: Beyond mortality, many mosquito-borne illnesses cause chronic complications (neurologic impacts, long recovery, recurrent infections). Removing the vector is seen as eliminating a major source of lifelong harm.

2) Economic gains and poverty reduction

From this perspective, mosquitoes are not just a health nuisance but an economic “tax” on entire regions.

  • Higher productivity: Fewer sick days, fewer caretaking burdens, and less long-term impairment translate into more stable work and schooling.
  • Lower healthcare spending: Countries and households spend enormous sums on treatment, prevention, and outbreak response (bed nets, insecticides, hospitalizations). Eradication is argued to be cheaper in the long run than perpetual control.
  • More investment and tourism: Areas associated with mosquito-borne disease can face reduced travel, higher insurance costs, and lower foreign investment. Removing the risk is pitched as unlocking growth.

3) Relief from constant prevention and surveillance

A big part of the “benefit” is the end of continuous defensive living.

  • Reduced reliance on pesticides and repellents: Advocates argue eradication would lessen chronic chemical use (sprays, coils, treated nets), along with associated costs and exposure concerns.
  • Less public-health strain: Vector control programs, outbreak monitoring, and emergency campaigns consume ongoing governmental capacity; eradication is framed as permanently freeing those resources.

4) Improved quality of life and livability

If mosquitoes are assumed to have no redeeming value, then everyday comfort becomes a legitimate primary goal.

  • Better sleep and mental well-being: Constant biting, buzzing, and fear of infection creates stress and sleep disruption; eradication is portrayed as immediate, universal relief.
  • Expanded outdoor activity: People avoid evenings outdoors, limit recreation, and change housing design because of mosquitoes. Removing them is seen as improving daily life and community life.

5) Benefits to animals, agriculture, and food security

In this framing, mosquitoes are also vectors and stressors beyond humans.

  • Reduced livestock disease and losses: Mosquito-borne infections can affect cattle, horses, and other animals; eradication is pitched as improving animal health and farm income.
  • More stable food production: Healthier farm labor and animals, plus fewer outbreak disruptions, are presented as indirect supports to food security.

6) A “solvable” target for global coordination

Advocates often argue mosquitoes are a uniquely compelling eradication target because they are identifiable, widespread, and tied to clear metrics.

  • Clear outcomes: Fewer mosquitoes → fewer bites → fewer cases. That causal chain makes the goal easy to communicate politically.
  • High return on investment: Because mosquito-borne diseases impose huge burdens, removing the vector is framed as one of the most cost-effective ways to improve global health.

7) The underlying moral argument (in this worldview)

Assuming mosquitoes have no redeeming value, proponents argue:

  • Net harm is overwhelming: Any hypothetical ecological role is treated as replaceable or insignificant compared with the scale of human suffering.
  • Involuntary risk is unacceptable: People do not consent to being exposed to biting and disease; eliminating the source is framed as a moral obligation analogous to removing other hazardous pests.

In short, from the “no redeeming values” perspective, a global mosquito-eradication campaign is justified as a direct, permanent intervention to eliminate a major driver of preventable disease and economic stagnation, while improving day-to-day human comfort and reducing the need for endless defensive measures.

  • They gasp, clutch pearls, and whisper, “But… the ecosystem.”

And if the ecosystem is so fragile that it collapses without a flying syringe whose main hobby is transmitting disease and making you look like you lost a fight with a pepper shaker, then maybe the ecosystem needs to hit the gym.

“You Can’t Play God!”

This is a popular one, usually said by people who:

  • wear glasses (technology),
  • use antibiotics (technology),
  • get vaccines (technology),
  • drive cars (technology),
  • live indoors (an affront to nature),
  • and have never once apologized to the gods for installing air conditioning.

The “Don’t Play God” crowd is not actually against playing god. They’re against playing god in a way that inconveniences their aesthetic of nature.

Because if we’re being honest, humanity already plays god constantly—we just call it “public health,” “infrastructure,” and “not dying of preventable nonsense.”

“But Think of the Food Chain!”

Yes. The food chain. The sacred ladder of life, where every creature has a role, and apparently mosquitos are an irreplaceable key link.

This is always framed as if removing mosquitos would cause birds to fall out of the sky like unplugged Wi‑Fi routers.

Meanwhile, actual birds are famously not picky. Birds will eat:

  • worms,
  • beetles,
  • seeds,
  • bread crumbs,
  • other birds,
  • a French fry they found in a parking lot,
  • the concept of “personal space.”

But sure—without mosquitos, the entire avian world will gather in a tiny feathered committee and formally resign.

“Eradicating a Species Is Immoral!”

This is the argument that really sings, because it’s typically delivered by someone actively attempting to eradicate:

  • bedbugs,
  • termites,
  • cockroaches,
  • head lice,
  • ticks,
  • and any spider that commits the unforgivable sin of existing within a three-foot radius of their shower.

The logic seems to be:

  • If it bites you and is hard to see: kill it with fire.
  • If it bites you, is hard to see, spreads malaria, and ruins every outdoor activity: a precious angel of nature.

Mosquitos have achieved an extraordinary public relations milestone: they are perhaps the only creature on Earth defended primarily by people who do not personally spend time with them.

“Just Use Bug Spray!”

Yes, because the humane solution is that I should:

  • marinate myself in chemicals,
  • dress like I’m going beekeeping,
  • avoid dusk, wetlands, shade, sun, still air, moving air, joy,
  • and schedule my entire existence around an insect whose life goal is to locate my ankles.

This is like responding to “We should fix potholes” with “Just buy a monster truck.”

Absolutely. Some mosquitos pollinate.

In the same way that a burglar might occasionally straighten a picture frame while robbing your house.

If mosquitos were applying for a job and listed “pollination” under skills, you’d still reject them because under “experience” it would say:
Five million years of freelancing in blood extraction and disease logistics.

“Nature Is Beautiful!”

Nature is beautiful. But nature is also:

  • rabies,
  • parasites,
  • fungus that eats frogs alive,
  • the concept of “predation,”
  • and a thousand ways to die that we have spent centuries politely declining.

People romanticize nature the way they romanticize the “simple life,” meaning: with no intention of actually living it.

A Modest Proposal: If You Love Mosquitos So Much…

If you truly believe mosquitos are misunderstood, I encourage you to:

  • stand outside in humid weather near still water,
  • wear shorts,
  • use no repellent,
  • and meditate on your principles for fifteen minutes.

If you emerge serene and unbitten, congratulations—you are either enlightened or a lizard.

If you emerge looking like a topographical map of itch, welcome to the great human tradition of realizing you were wrong in a way that leaves welts.

Want to defend a maligned creature? Defend sharks. Defend bats. Defend snakes. These animals do important work and mostly want to be left alone.

Mosquitos do not want to be left alone.
Mosquitos want access to your bloodstream and a standing reservation at your eardrum.

If we can end that relationship, it won’t be “playing god.”
It’ll be setting boundaries.
